name: Linear Operator
meaning: A rule taking vectors to vectors while respecting addition and scaling.
formal: $A(a|u\rangle+b|v\rangle)=aA|u\rangle+bA|v\rangle$. The input vectors must belong to the operator domain.
example: $A(x,y)=(2x,3y)$ is linear. $A(x)=x^2$ is not linear over real numbers.
linkedFormal: $A(a|u\rangle+b|v\rangle)=aA|u\rangle+bA|v\rangle$. The input [[Vector|vectors]] must belong to the [[Operator Domain|operator domain]].

name: Operator Domain
meaning: The set of vectors on which an operator is defined.
formal: $D(A)$ is the set of allowed inputs of $A$. For a derivative on square-integrable functions, extra differentiability and boundary conditions are required.
example: Not every square-integrable function has a square-integrable derivative.

check.prompt: Is a derivative defined on every square-integrable function?
check.explanation: Some such functions are not differentiable.

linkedFormal: $D(A)$ is the [[Set|set]] of allowed inputs of $A$. For a [[Derivative|derivative]] on square-integrable functions, extra [[Derivative|differentiability]] and boundary conditions are required.

name: Operator Product
meaning: Apply one operator and then another.
formal: $(AB)|v\rangle=A(B|v\rangle)$ wherever both applications are defined. The rightmost operator acts first.

check.explanation: Read composition from right to left.

linkedFormal: $(AB)|v\rangle=A(B|v\rangle)$ wherever both applications are defined. The rightmost [[Linear Operator|operator]] acts first.

name: Identity Operator
meaning: The operator that leaves every vector unchanged.
example: Its two-dimensional matrix has diagonal entries 1 and off-diagonal entries 0.

name: Hermitian Adjoint
meaning: The operator obtained by moving an operation across an inner product.
formal: $\langle u|Av\rangle=\langle A^\dagger u|v\rangle$ for allowed vectors. For matrices, $(A^\dagger)_{ij}=A_{ji}^*$.

check.prompt: How do you find a matrix adjoint?

linkedFormal: $\langle u|Av\rangle=\langle A^\dagger u|v\rangle$ for allowed [[Vector|vectors]]. For matrices, $(A^\dagger)_{ij}=A_{ji}^*$.

name: Hermitian Operator
meaning: An operator equal to its adjoint in the setting under consideration.
formal: In finite dimensions, Hermitian means $A=A^\dagger$, equivalently $\langle u|Av\rangle=\langle Au|v\rangle$. For unbounded operators, distinguish this symmetry identity from self-adjointness, which also requires equality of domains.

check.explanation: Match the matrix to its conjugate transpose.

linkedFormal: In finite dimensions, Hermitian means $A=A^\dagger$, equivalently $\langle u|Av\rangle=\langle Au|v\rangle$. For [[Operator Domain|unbounded]] operators, distinguish this [[Symmetric Operator|symmetry identity]] from [[Self-adjoint Operator|self-adjointness]], which also requires equality of domains.

name: Self-adjoint Operator
meaning: An operator matching its adjoint in both action and allowed inputs.
formal: $A=A^\dagger$ and $D(A)=D(A^\dagger)$. In finite dimensions this is the same as being Hermitian.
example: The momentum derivative requires a suitable domain and boundary conditions to be self-adjoint.

check.prompt: For an unbounded self-adjoint operator, domains must…
check.explanation: Matching the formula alone is insufficient.

linkedFormal: $A=A^\dagger$ and $D(A)=D(A^\dagger)$. In finite dimensions this is the same as being [[Hermitian Operator|Hermitian]].

name: Commutator
meaning: The difference between applying two operators in opposite orders.
formal: $[A,B]=AB-BA$. Commuting operators satisfy $[A,B]=0$. The product rule is $[A,BC]=[A,B]C+B[A,C]$.
example: $[x,p]=i\hbar I$ in the canonical position–momentum setting.
linkedFormal: $[A,B]=AB-BA$. Commuting operators satisfy $[A,B]=0$. The product rule is $[A,BC]=[A,B]C+B[A,C]$.

name: Anticommutator
meaning: The sum of two operator products in opposite orders.

name: Function of an Operator
meaning: A function evaluated with an operator in place of its input.
formal: For a polynomial, $f(A)=\sum_{n=0}^{N}c_nA^n$ with $A^0=I$. A power series requires convergence; more general definitions need a suitable spectral construction.

check.explanation: The constant term multiplies the identity.

linkedFormal: For a [[Polynomial|polynomial]], $f(A)=\sum_{n=0}^{N}c_nA^n$ with $A^0=I$. A power series requires [[Convergence|convergence]]; more general definitions need a suitable spectral construction.

name: Position Operator
meaning: The operator that multiplies a position wave function by its coordinate.
formal: $(\hat x\psi)(x)=x\psi(x)$ on the domain with $x\psi\in L^2$.

check.prompt: In position space, x̂ acts by…
check.explanation: The coordinate is the position eigenvalue.

linkedFormal: $(\hat x\psi)(x)=x\psi(x)$ on the domain with $x\psi\in L^2$.

name: Momentum Operator
meaning: The operator that differentiates a position wave function with a quantum scale factor.
formal: $(\hat p\psi)(x)=-i\hbar\,d\psi/dx$ on a suitable domain. A plane wave $e^{ipx/\hbar}$ satisfies $\hat p e^{ipx/\hbar}=p e^{ipx/\hbar}$.

check.prompt: In position space, p̂ acts as…

linkedFormal: $(\hat p\psi)(x)=-i\hbar\,d\psi/dx$ on a suitable domain. A plane wave $e^{ipx/\hbar}$ satisfies $\hat p e^{ipx/\hbar}=p e^{ipx/\hbar}$.

name: Symmetric Operator
meaning: An operator whose action can move across an inner product on its own domain.
formal: $\langle u|Av\rangle=\langle Au|v\rangle$ for all $u,v\in D(A)$. For unbounded operators this need not imply $D(A)=D(A^\dagger)$, so it need not imply self-adjointness.
example: A derivative can satisfy the symmetry identity on a restricted domain without being self-adjoint.

check.prompt: Does symmetry alone settle self-adjointness for unbounded operators?
options: Only if the eigenvalues are integers
check.explanation: The adjoint domain may be larger.

linkedFormal: $\langle u|Av\rangle=\langle Au|v\rangle$ for all $u,v\in D(A)$. For [[Operator Domain|unbounded]] operators this need not imply $D(A)=D(A^\dagger)$, so it need not imply [[Self-adjoint Operator|self-adjointness]].

name: Antisymmetric Part
meaning: The half-difference between two opposite-order products.
formal: $AB=\tfrac12(AB+BA)+\tfrac12(AB-BA)$. The second term is the antisymmetric part under swapping $A,B$.
example: It changes sign when A and B are exchanged.

check.prompt: Swapping A and B changes the antisymmetric part’s sign to…

linkedFormal: $AB=\tfrac12(AB+BA)+\tfrac12(AB-BA)$. The second term is the antisymmetric part under swapping $A,B$.

name: Symmetric Part
meaning: The half-sum of two opposite-order products.
formal: The symmetric part is $\tfrac12(AB+BA)$ and is unchanged under exchanging $A$ and $B$.

check.prompt: The symmetric part of AB is…

linkedFormal: The symmetric part is $\tfrac12(AB+BA)$ and is unchanged under exchanging $A$ and $B$.
